summary.text: Fish are water-living vertebrates that breathe with gills and have a tough skull protecting the brain.
There are over 33,000 living species, more than amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals combined, and most belong to the ray-finned class.
Because four-limbed land vertebrates descend from fish, modern classification no longer treats fish as one class, and the old name Pisces is retired.

items.prompt: A dolphin has a streamlined, fish-like body. What best explains that?

options.label: It is a jawless fish that kept an ancient body plan
It is a cartilaginous fish that learned to breathe air
It belongs to a four-limbed vertebrate group that took on the shape separately
It is a ray-finned fish with unusually large fins

items.explain: Cetaceans are tetrapods that acquired a fish-like body shape through convergent evolution, so the look does not make them fish.

items.prompt: You pick one living fish species at random. Which kind is it most likely to be?

options.label: A ray-finned fish able to protrude its jaws
A cartilaginous fish with a flexible skeleton
A jawless fish with a round mouth
A lobe-finned fish with fleshy fins

items.explain: Teleosts, a group of ray-finned fish that can protrude their jaws, make up about 96% of living fish species.

items.prompt: A scientist insists the word "fish" must name one complete branch of the family tree, with every descendant of the earliest fish included. What follows?

options.label: Sharks and rays would have to be dropped from the group
Only fish that have jaws could still be called fish
Fish would have to be split into three separate classes
Land animals would count as fish, so "fish" would mean the same as "vertebrates"

items.explain: Tetrapods descend from fish, so a complete branch of fish would include them, making "fish" and "vertebrates" synonyms.

items.prompt: An aquarium sign reads: "Tank 1: twenty clownfish. Tank 2: a clownfish, a pufferfish and an angelfish." Which wording follows how biologists use the words?

options.label: Tank 1 holds fishes; Tank 2 holds fish
Tank 1 holds fish; Tank 2 holds fishes
Both tanks hold fish
Both tanks hold fishes

items.explain: Fish is the plural for individuals of one species, while fishes describes different species.

items.prompt: In which period did fish diversity greatly increase, earning it a nickname about fish?

options.label: The Cambrian
The Silurian
The Devonian
The Carboniferous

items.explain: The Devonian saw placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks diversify, so it is called the age of fishes.

items.prompt: Cold water around a reef cools sharply overnight. Which fish would most likely keep its core warmer than the water?

options.label: A large, fast-swimming tuna
A small reef fish that hovers in one spot
A bottom-dweller resting in the shallows
Any fish, since every fish is warm-blooded

items.explain: Most fish are cold-blooded, but some large, active swimmers like tuna and the white shark hold a higher core temperature.

pack.title: Is "fish" even a thing?
pack.question: Why do biologists say "fish" is not one tidy group?

beats.title: Is "fish" even a thing?
beats.hook: Your own ancestors were fish, which makes the word surprisingly hard to define.

beats.prompt: Imagine one branch of the family tree that holds the earliest fish and every one of their descendants. Where would humans sit?
beats.explain: Tetrapods, including humans, are modified bony fishes. A branch holding every descendant of the first fish would include us, and "fish" would match "vertebrates".

choices.label: Inside it, because tetrapods descend from fish
Outside it, because our ancestors left the water long ago
choices.feedback: Leaving the water does not remove a lineage from its ancestry: tetrapods still descend from fish.

choices.label: On a separate branch, because we breathe with lungs
choices.feedback: It tempts because lungs seem new, but tetrapod lungs are homologous to swim bladders, which fish already had.

beats.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.label: Four-limbed vertebrates, mostly living on land
Ray-finned fish that can protrude their jaws

beats.explain: Each term names a piece of the fish story, from the science itself to the land vertebrates that grew out of it.

beats.prompt: Add up every living species of amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. How does that total compare with living fish species?
beats.explain: With over 33,000 living species, fish are easily the largest group of vertebrates, more than the other four traditional classes combined.

choices.label: The two totals are roughly equal
choices.feedback: Fish are not close to a tie: with over 33,000 species they pass the other four classes combined.

choices.label: Fish alone outnumber all four classes combined
The four land-linked classes together are far larger
choices.feedback: Mammals and birds get the attention, but they are small groups next to fish.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Four-limbed land vertebrates evolved from lobe-finned fish.
So any group containing all jawed fish must also contain those land vertebrates.
So fish, leaving them out, form a paraphyletic group.
That is why Pisces is still the standard formal class for fish.

beats.explain: Because fish without tetrapods are paraphyletic, the class Pisces from older reference works is no longer used in formal classifications.

beats.idea: Since four-limbed land vertebrates descend from fish, "fish" covers every vertebrate except them and is a handy label, not a complete branch of the family tree.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a fish
paragraphs.text: A fish is a vertebrate that lives in water, breathes with gills and has a tough skull, the cranium, guarding its brain. Many fish have fins that keep them on course and push them along. Most are cold-blooded, so their body temperature rises and falls with the water around them. A few large, fast swimmers such as the white shark and tuna can keep their core warmer. The science of fish is called ichthyology.

paragraphs.heading: A huge and varied group
paragraphs.text: More than 33,000 living species of fish are known, more than amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals put together. Most of them are ray-finned fishes, a class that alone makes up about half of all living vertebrates. Within it, the teleosts, fish that can push their jaws forward, account for about 96% of living fish species. Sizes run from the whale shark at 16 metres down to tiny teleosts only 8 millimetres long, such as Paedocypris progenetica.

paragraphs.heading: Bony fish take over
paragraphs.text: Bony fish carry a swim bladder, and later ones also have skeletons made of bone. They became the leading group after an extinction at the end of the Devonian wiped out the placoderms, which had been the top predators. Bony fish split into two branches, the lobe-finned and the ray-finned fishes. During the Carboniferous, lobe-finned fish gave rise to the tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates that mostly live on land, and their air-breathing lungs correspond to the swim bladder.

paragraphs.heading: Why fish is not one class
paragraphs.text: Older books put every fish into a single class called Pisces, but that class is no longer used in formal classification. The reason is that tetrapods descend from fish. Any group that includes all bony fish therefore also includes the tetrapods, so fish without them is what biologists call a paraphyletic group. To make fish one complete branch, tetrapods would have to count as specialised fish, and fish would simply mean vertebrate. The reference book Fishes of the World accepts this, calling tetrapods, humans included, modified bony fishes.

paragraphs.heading: Fish, fishes and people
paragraphs.text: In biology, fish and fishes mean different things: fish names one or more individual animals, while fishes names different species. People have relied on fish since prehistoric times, especially as food. Fish are caught in the wild or raised in ponds and ocean cages. They are also caught for sport, kept in aquariums and garden ponds, and have appeared as gods, religious symbols and subjects of art, books and films.
